scholars.dates: Flourished in the 9th century CE; exact life dates not established
scholars.biography: Aḥmad al-Farghānī was an astronomer active in the Abbasid world during the ninth century. His best-known surviving work is a concise compendium of Ptolemaic astronomy, composed after 833 and before 857 according to its biographical-encyclopedia entry. Its Arabic and Latin transmission made it influential in medieval Europe. A treatise on the mathematical principles of the astrolabe also survives. Later associations with the Nilometer at al-Fusṭāṭ and an Iraqi canal are recorded by the source, but the biographical details are sparse and those projects should not be treated as certain personal authorship without further evidence.

contributions.prior: Ptolemy’s Almagest and the Arabic astronomical tradition
contributions.detail: The BEA dates its composition between 833 and 857 and documents Arabic, Hebrew, and Latin transmission.

scholars.biography: Thābit ibn Qurra was a Harranian scholar who worked in Baghdad and wrote in Arabic, with some works in Syriac. The Dictionary of Scientific Biography describes his fluency in Syriac, Greek, and Arabic and his invitation to Baghdad by Muḥammad ibn Mūsā ibn Shākir, linking his career to the Banū Mūsā circle. His work included translations and commentaries on Greek mathematics, original geometry and number theory, and mathematical astronomy. Some titles attributed to him have later been judged misattributions, so an author’s name in a transmitted title is not by itself proof of authorship.

scholars.biography: Al-Battānī, known in Latin sources as Albategnius, was an astronomer and mathematician whose Zij preserves systematic astronomical work in the Ptolemaic tradition. The Dictionary of Scientific Biography documents the work’s later use by medieval Latin authors and by early modern astronomers including Copernicus and Tycho Brahe. This reception history shows transmission and influence; it does not imply that the historical model in the Zij is identical to modern astronomy. His exact life dates are not harmonized here because reference accounts differ.

contributions.title: Astronomical observations and tables in the Zij
contributions.text: Al-Battānī’s Zij was used by later astronomers and became known through Latin transmission. ISA records this as observational and tabular astronomy; claims about particular numerical innovations require checking a critical edition of the tables.
contributions.prior: Ptolemaic astronomical parameters and earlier zij traditions
contributions.detail: Influence documented in the DSB entry; detailed parameter comparisons remain future work.

scholars.dates: 940–997/998 CE; DSB gives death as 997 or July 998
scholars.biography: Abū al-Wafāʾ was born in Būzjān and moved to Baghdad in 959, where he worked in mathematics and astronomy. The DSB describes a practical arithmetic textbook for scribes, merchants, finance clerks, and surveyors, alongside commentaries and astronomical work. It notes that he made accurate trigonometric tables and contributed to spherical trigonometry, while also cautioning that a proposed direct influence on later European trigonometry has not been established. His death date is uncertain in the source.

contributions.text: His arithmetic manual systematized practical calculation and criticized some methods as inaccurate; the DSB also documents work on trigonometry and accurate tables. ISA classifies this as mathematical development and exposition, not a claim of sole invention of trigonometry.
contributions.prior: Earlier Greek and Indian arithmetic and the Arabic mathematical tradition
contributions.detail: The DSB cautions that the exact relationship between his work and later European trigonometry remains unsettled.

scholars.biography: Ibn Sīnā was a philosopher and physician whose career unfolded amid shifting political patronage in the eastern Islamic lands. His Canon of Medicine organized a wide body of medical knowledge in five books and became influential as a teaching text. Encyclopaedia Iranica emphasizes that the Canon built on the Galenic medical tradition and on earlier Arabic medical writing, including work by Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq and al-Rāzī; it should therefore be described as a major synthesis and systematization, not as the origin of medicine. His philosophical and scientific writings extended beyond medicine, while dates in the biographical record remain approximate.

contributions.prior: Galenic medicine and earlier Arabic medical compendia
contributions.detail: Influence and exact reception vary by region and period; no modern clinical validity is implied for medieval medical theory.

scholars.biography: Al-Bīrūnī was a scholar of Khwarazm whose work ranged across astronomy, mathematics, geography, physics, chronology, and the study of India. The St Andrews biographical account describes him as a careful observer attentive to measurement error and as a scholar who studied Sanskrit texts directly. Among the works discussed are the Chronology of Ancient Nations, India, the Masʿūdī Canon, and writings on shadows and geodesy. This profile avoids turning isolated observations into modern discoveries: each claim about a measurement or technique requires its own textual and numerical verification.

contributions.prior: Earlier Greek, Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit geographical and astronomical traditions
contributions.detail: Specific measurement claims need direct checking against critical editions and modern geodesy.

scholars.dates: c. 965–1040 CE; life details are disputed
scholars.biography: Ibn al-Haytham, known in Latin as Alhazen, worked in mathematics and natural philosophy and is especially associated with optics. Sources disagree about elements of his biography, including the story of his Nile project and later confinement, so those details are not stated as fact here. The DSB catalogues a large body of optical, mathematical, and astronomical writing and explicitly identifies several works that were falsely attributed to him. His profile therefore treats authorship as a bibliographical question and avoids the popular but misleading label “the first scientist.”

contributions.text: Ibn al-Haytham’s optical writing critically examined theories of vision and the propagation of light. This profile records the historical work as an important contribution to optics without implying that its full framework matches modern physical optics.
contributions.prior: Greek optical theories, including those associated with Euclid and Ptolemy
contributions.detail: Claims about experiments and specific results should be anchored to the Arabic text and the DSB bibliography; the manuscript tradition includes works of uncertain authorship.

scholars.biography: Al-Zahrāwī was an Andalusian physician associated with Córdoba and best known for the medical encyclopedia Kitāb al-Taṣrīf. The work is described in modern medical-historical literature as a multi-part compendium, with the final section devoted to surgery. It gathered medical practice and knowledge of its period and later circulated in Latin translation. The ISA record does not label him “the father of surgery” or call particular instruments first inventions: those claims require closer study of the text, earlier sources, and transmission history.

contributions.prior: Greek, late antique, and earlier Arabic medical traditions
contributions.detail: The cited review supports the broad work description; individual procedures and instruments need primary-text and specialist verification.

scholars.dates: 1210/1213–1288 CE; birth year differs across modern accounts
scholars.biography: Ibn al-Nafīs was a physician and jurist who studied in Damascus and later worked in Cairo. His Commentary on the Anatomy of Avicenna’s Canon rejects the Galenic passage through the interventricular septum and describes blood moving from the right ventricle through the lungs to the left side of the heart. Modern historians and physiologists discuss this as an important description of pulmonary transit, while the history of its later transmission to European writers remains uncertain. A modern medical-historical article reports that a copy of the commentary was identified in Berlin as manuscript 912; ISA has not inspected that manuscript directly.

contributions.title: Description of pulmonary transit in the heart and lungs
contributions.text: In his commentary on Avicenna’s anatomical text, Ibn al-Nafīs argued that blood does not pass through visible or invisible pores in the cardiac septum and instead passes through the lungs before reaching the left side. This is a historical anatomical description; questions of priority and influence on later European accounts are treated cautiously.
contributions.prior: Galenic cardiac anatomy and its later Arabic reception
contributions.detail: A modern physiology paper attributes a major early description to Ibn al-Nafīs; direct manuscript examination and transmission evidence remain outside this project’s review.

scholars.biography: Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq was a physician and a leading translator of Greek works into Arabic and Syriac. The DSB describes his close attention to translation quality, his work with his son Isḥāq and other collaborators, and his translations of Hippocratic, Galenic, and other medical texts. Translation in this period involved revising versions against multiple manuscripts and was a collaborative scholarly practice, rather than simple word-for-word copying. Hunayn was a Syriac Christian scholar working within the diverse intellectual culture of Abbasid Baghdad.

contributions.detail: Attribution of specific translations can be collaborative; the DSB entry should be checked title by title before a complete works catalogue is attempted.

scholars.biography: Al-Rāzī was a physician, philosopher, and author from Rayy. Encyclopaedia Iranica describes al-Ḥāwī as a large medical work compiled after his death from notes and commonplace books, rather than a finished encyclopedia authored in its surviving form. His writing on smallpox and measles and his extensive pharmacological material are important parts of the medical record. The profile distinguishes his historical medical system from modern clinical knowledge and avoids repeating popular claims about “firsts” without a precise textual basis.

ISA classifies the encyclopedic work as synthesis and records its posthumous compilation history.

ala_hazrat_updates.biography: Imam Ahmad Raza Khan (1856–1921), widely known as Ala Hazrat, was a Hanafi scholar and a leading figure in South Asian Sunni religious life under British rule. Usha Sanyal’s academic study situates his thought in the social and political history of late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century India. A 2023 descriptive bibliography by Imad Jafar inventories 200 published works and explicitly notes that it is not exhaustive. A 2026 Urdu-language study argues that Khan also engaged with arithmetic, geometry, algebra, trigonometry, logarithms, and astronomical tables; because its linked full text was not read and no individual calculation has been checked, ISA records those subjects as a research lead rather than as verified scientific achievements. His earth-motion treatises are presented as historical religious and natural-philosophical arguments. Modern astronomy is assessed independently and respectfully, without presenting his historical conclusion as current scientific consensus.
ala_hazrat_updates.works_catalogue_note: The existing six-item catalogue is a provisional selection, not a complete works list. Jafar (2023, pp. 545–560) provides a descriptive bibliography of 200 published works and reports that many more exist; the article itself says it does not give first-print details for every title. Cataloguing should proceed against that bibliography and library records. No total oeuvre count is asserted by ISA.
